blocks.text: Involvement of the anorectal mucosa in addition to the anal sphincter complex.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. When should you perform a rectal examination?

blocks.text: When an OASI is suspected and after repair to ensure the rectal mucosa has not been inadvertently sutured.

content_groups.group_title: Q8. What is the most important long-term complication of OASI?

blocks.text: **Anal incontinence**, including flatus or faecal incontinence.

content_groups.group_title: Q9. What are the risk factors for OASI?

blocks.text: Operative vaginal delivery, especially forceps, large baby, first vaginal birth, persistent occipitoposterior position, shoulder dystocia and previous OASI.

content_groups.group_title: Q10. What would you do if the patient is unstable?

blocks.text: ABCDE resuscitation, call senior help, obtain IV access, activate major haemorrhage protocol when indicated, give blood products as required, identify the source rapidly and proceed to urgent surgical control.

**“This is primary postpartum haemorrhage with a firm, well-contracted uterus, so I am particularly concerned about genital tract trauma. I would call for senior obstetric and anaesthetic assistance while continuing ABCDE resuscitation and obtaining IV access and blood investigations. I would inspect the perineum and episiotomy site, examine the vagina for lacerations or haematoma and assess the cervix if there is no obvious source. If an obstetric anal sphincter injury is suspected, I would classify it accurately and perform a rectal examination. Significant tears would require appropriate repair under adequate analgesia or anaesthesia, with senior involvement. I would continue monitoring and blood-product resuscitation as required.”**
